posts.name: Johns Charts
posts.text: “Spend more time studying the conditions that make your setups work and less time obsessing over the perfect entry”- @RealSimpleAriel

quoted.text:
WHEN > WHERE

So many people want to fight for pennies on a big-picture trade idea.

When you take the time to study the daily chart and understand your playbook, whether you’re buying a support gap, a 6/20 setup, a VWAP reclaim, a 5-minute ORB or a break of the prior day’s high, these are relatively small nuances in the grand scheme of things.

Yes, I’m aware that certain entries allow for tighter risk management and potentially larger position sizes.

BUT, and this is the more important part, are you recognizing what is going on around you that would create the conditions necessary for your trade idea to actually work?

Over time, you’ll come to learn that WHEN you buy something is far more important than WHERE you bought it.

Show up to buy $SMH or $GLD after 10 a.m. today and you’re likely making money regardless of which entry technique you employed. But show up to buy those same names 2, 4 or 10 days ago, and you could have been getting destroyed because you failed to recognize that it wasn’t the proper “WHEN.”

You can have a textbook entry in the wrong environment and still lose money. Conversely, you can have a mediocre entry in the right environment and make a lot of money.

Spend more time studying the conditions that make your setups work and less time obsessing over the perfect entry.

Something to stew on over the holiday weekend. 🦃

Rumors floating around that $APP might be looking to buy $PINS ... personally I hope it happens but only if $APP is going to do some significant layoffs and other cost cutting measures.

Currently, $APP does 75% more revenues than $PINS with 80% less employees.

$APP is one of the most efficient publicly traded companies... with ~84% ebitda margins... which translates into almost $8 million per employee.

$PINS has ~30% ebitda margins. 

$PINS will do $4.8 billion in revenues this year with ~4,000 employees 

$APP will do $8.4 billion in revenues this year with ~900 employees.

I'm not an expert in $PINS or their tech stack but I know $APP quite well and I think this marriage could work especially with $APP pushing harder into ecommerce where $PINS and their customer data should be very beneficial. 

Fast forward to 2028, the combination of $APP + $PINS could be doing $16+ billion in ebitda which might be worth $250-300 billion which is more than double their current combined market caps.

Feel free to share your thoughts.

posts.name: Jose Najarro Stocks
posts.text:
CoreWeave $CRWV is reportedly about to borrow like an investment grade company while its own bonds trade like junk: its banks plan to sell a loan of up to $4.5B backed by GPUs dedicated to Meta as soon as next week, per Bloomberg.

Per Bloomberg, Morgan Stanley and MUFG are running the deal, the money sits in escrow to buy GPUs for a data center in Dalton, Georgia, and the loan pays down over its life. It's expected to get investment grade ratings because of the Meta contract behind it, and there's reportedly already interest for the full amount. Pricing talk is a 7% to 7.5% yield, while CoreWeave's 2031 bonds were yielding close to 18% this morning, per Tradeweb data.

This is exactly what management promised. "We expect to launch our next DDTL in the coming weeks. This will be an investment-grade facility with multiple rating agencies indicating a high investment-grade rating," CoreWeave said on its Nov. 10 call, adding it would not use the unsecured bond market at current yields.

Why it matters: this morning's story was CoreWeave's credit getting priced like distress. This is the other side of the neocloud model. The company's credit is weak, but Meta's is strong, and lenders are lending against the customer, not the borrower. With about $46.9B of debt on the balance sheet at the end of September, CoreWeave needs that door to stay open. If this prices near the talk, the GPU orders for Georgia keep moving. Nothing is final until it prices.

posts.name: Jose Najarro Stocks
posts.text:
Taiwan Semiconductor $TSM and the AI hardware chain got a big carve out in Washington's new tariff push: chips, servers, server boards, network switches and chipmaking tools are all on the exemption list.

USTR on Wednesday proposed Section 301 tariffs on 14 economies over what it calls "structural excess capacity." Taiwan and Korea each face up to 15% including normal duties, with a fallback of up to 25% if USTR decides ongoing talks fall short. Malaysia is up to 18%, China up to 20% and Vietnam up to 35%. Mexico got no determination for now.

The fine print is the story for AI. Semiconductor articles are exempt because they already sit under the Section 232 chip tariffs, and the Taiwan, Korea and Malaysia annexes also exclude computers and processing units (the server codes), their circuit board assemblies, switching and routing gear, and semiconductor manufacturing equipment. USTR still calls out Taiwan's support for high tech manufacturing and warns that over reliance on a single economy for semiconductors "increases the cost of any disruption."

Chips are getting crushed today anyway, with the selloff tied to AI spending doubts, the tariff headlines and rising Fed hike bets. My read: these proposals are not a direct hit on AI data center hardware. Nothing is final yet, and the proposals are open for public comment into January.

posts.name: Jose Najarro Stocks
posts.text:
SpaceX $SPCX just got the first US license ever for a full constellation of data centers in space: the FCC authorized up to 1 million "Starmind" orbital compute satellites.

The order comes with hard deadlines. SpaceX needs one satellite operating by Nov. 25, 2033, 10% of the fleet by 2035, 50% by 2038 and all of it by 2040, or the authorization goes void. The satellites fly in shells from 500 to 1,002 km, move data over laser links into Starlink, and only get Ka-band radio as a backup. The FCC also denied petitions to block it from Amazon's Kuiper, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society.

"By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said.

The fine print: the debris plan was only approved for satellites below 600 km. SpaceX's request to dispose of higher satellites without burning them up in the atmosphere was deferred, so anything above 600 km needs another filing first. And a license is not a launch. The first deadline is still seven years out.

Why it matters: on Earth, data centers are stuck waiting on power, land and permits. SpaceX pitches Starmind as a way to "capture solar energy in space to power" AI, per The Verge, and it already owns the rockets and the network. Google already launched its first Suncatcher AI server satellite, per The Verge, and the FCC says it is reviewing more orbital data center proposals. The race for compute just left the atmosphere.

$NVDA $GOOGL $AMZN $TSM

posts.name: Dividendology
posts.text:
I recently interviewed Dwayne Hyzak, the CEO of Main Street Capital $MAIN-

Which is possibly the greatest monthly dividend paying stocks of all time.

Main Street makes money by providing both debt and equity capital to mature, owner-operated businesses in the lower middle market.

That earns it recurring interest income, plus a share of the upside when those companies grow.

This has led to susbstaintale outperformance since they went public.

And according to Dwayne, one of Main Street’s biggest advantages right now comes from what it does NOT own:

Software.

When I asked about Main Street’s software exposure, he said:

“If there’s an area, or a couple of areas, that we are underexposed to, one of those would be software.”

That’s by design.

Main Street focuses on basic, mature companies, businesses that have “been around for decades, not years.”

Then he added:

“We probably got criticized for not having more exposure to software historically. I think clearly today we view that as a strength and a benefit.”

Meanwhile, many other BDCs spent the last five years leaning into software-

A space that’s come under serious pressure over the last year, largely because of AI.

Now, according to Dwayne, those BDCs are shifting toward basic industrial businesses that “look and feel more like what Main Street has always invested in.”

When I asked whether AI has changed how Main Street underwrites deals, his answer was simple:

“We’re not big software guys, so it’s not like AI is going to fundamentally change the vast majority of the companies that we either invest in or that we look at.”

AI can help someone build competing software…

But it can’t recreate a manufacturer or distributor with decades of customer relationships behind it.

Sometimes the most “boring” businesses are the hardest to disrupt.

Dwayne and I also talked about Main Street’s dividend policy, how they decide on the supplemental dividend, why issuing shares above NAV can benefit shareholders, and where he sees the company 10 years from now.

posts.text:
$VLO $MPC $PSX $DK $CLMT RUSSIAN REFINERY RUNS DROP TO LOWEST IN DECADES, RYSTAD SAYS

THE ESTIMATE
• Rystad Energy puts Russian refinery runs at 2.6 to 2.7 million barrels a day as of Monday, roughly halving since Oct. 30 and the lowest in more than two decades
• Rystad calculates runs by monitoring crude-supply chains, tanker tracking, satellite images and industry sources
• The estimate does not include the impact of Wednesday's strikes on two refineries in the Samara region
• Bloomberg's tally counts at least 18 refineries attacked since late October, though not all of the nameplate capacity hit is necessarily affected

THE CROSS-CHECKS
• Rystad's own ladder: 5.0 million barrels a day in late October, 4.2 million over the first ten days of November, now 2.6 to 2.7 million. The decline accelerated hard in the last two weeks
• The Ukraine_Data oil tracker, an independent bottom-up model, put runs at a 3.37 million barrel a day mid estimate on Nov. 19, inside a 2.6 to 4.35 million band, with its own crisis threshold at 2.8 million. Rystad's range sits at the bottom of that band and below that threshold
• Two independent methodologies converge on the same zone: the direction is high confidence, the exact level is one firm's estimate
• Against late-October runs, the Rystad range implies roughly 45 to 50% of Russian throughput is now offline. The Samara exclusion cuts less than the headline suggests: both Samara plants were already effectively offline, so Wednesday's strikes extend outages rather than removing running barrels

THE OFFICIAL SIGNAL
• President Putin said on Tuesday the situation on the domestic oil-product market "remains challenging"; Deputy Prime Minister Novak said on Wednesday the situation is "quite tense" (Tass)
• Average weekly retail gasoline prices rose 0.5% in the Nov. 17-23 period, the biggest weekly increase since early September (Federal Statistics Service)
• Gasoline and jet fuel export restrictions remain in place, fuel imports continue, and diesel supplies to global markets have been allowed only following an agreement with the US

THE MARKET SPLIT
• Crude Moscow cannot process is being diverted into the export stream, lifting overseas crude sales and adding to the global crude surplus
• The tight leg is products: Russian diesel, gasoline and jet supply is short, which supports product cracks into Europe and US Gulf Coast export arbs
• The offset in the US is a soft domestic print run: two straight EIA distillate builds, with the industry survey pointing to a third in the week just ended, and the front 3-2-1 crack printing 37.60 on Nov. 24
• Watch: the next Ukraine_Data tracker print against its 2.8 million barrel a day crisis line, Russian diesel export loadings, and any rationing or regional shortage headlines

This is actually insane.

Someone is willing to pay me $1,140 just for agreeing to buy $TSLA at $320 by January 15.

It's called a cash-secured put, and here's how it works.

TSLA is trading around $373. I sell the $320 put expiring January 15, 2027 and collect about $11.40 per share, or $1,140 for one contract.

That means I need $32,000 in cash set aside. That's where the "cash-secured" part comes from.

Two outcomes:

1. TSLA stays above $320 by expiration. I keep the $1,140, a 3.6% return on the cash in 51 days.

2. TSLA closes below $320. I buy 100 shares at $320, and the premium lowers my real cost to $308.60. That's about 17% below today's price.

Of course, there's risk. If TSLA drops to $250, I'd be down about $5,860 on the shares. Someone who bought 100 shares today would be down about $12,300.

Tesla's Q4 report usually lands in late January, after this put expires.

The stock is 25% off its 52-week high and implied volatility is 61%, which is why the premium is this rich.

posts.text:
AI agents are driving massive cybersecurity consolidation.

1️⃣ Palo Alto Networks saw it early with its $25B offer for CyberArk in July 2025.

Palo Alto started in network security. Over time it expanded into cloud, endpoint and SIEM. But it lacked identity.
 
CyberArk filled this void.
 
But CyberArk already had its act together, growing ARR 47% to $1.27B.
 
Hence, the higher but reasonable multiple: 19.6x ARR.

2️⃣ CrowdStrike is now expanding to the network with its $43.9B offer for Zscaler.

CrowdStrike started at the endpoint and added cloud, identity and SIEM.
 
Zscaler is a leader in network security, which CrowdStrike calls cyber's largest single market.
 
After close, Falcon covers the device an agent runs on and the network it connects through.
 
CrowdStrike says the deal adds $185B+ to its addressable market in 2029.
 
Zscaler had struggled with go-to-market, something CrowdStrike excels at.
 
While many view the $500M of cost and ~$1B of revenue synergies as aggressive, they may prove to be conservative.
 
CrowdStrike is buying Zscaler at 11.3x ARR, paying with its own stock valued at ~37x ARR.

3️⃣ Palo Alto is making another bold move to expand into AI models with its $4.5B offer for Applied Compute.

After CyberArk, Palo Alto already covers most of the cybersecurity map.
 
Applied Compute isn't on it. It helps enterprises train and run their own open-weight models.
 
Palo Alto says AI security must move "from visibility and enforcement to trust in the model itself."
 
It targets $1B of added ARR from the deal by fiscal 2029.
 
While the ~45x revenue run-rate multiple seems high at first sight, this is about acquiring a team and new technology, not necessarily ARR.

Enterprises want more control over their AI models, but they also need to trust them in production.
 
Pairing Applied Compute’s model-training team with Palo Alto’s security expertise could help address both needs.
 
All three deals point to a broader ambition: securing the identity, the network and the model behind an AI agent.
 
Sign up for Tech Edge, our weekly research newsletter, for more on all three deals (link in the comments).

$SPY has been higher 12 months after every midterm for decades, and the last two cycles both ripped out of the gate in January.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY GOING ON IN MARKETS

The data today was hot:
• Q3 GDP revised up to 4.3%
• Core PCE 3.3%, highest since 2023
• Jobless claims 189k

A December Fed hike is fully priced. Futures see rates peaking near 4.50% by June.

Normally that sends bond yields UP. Instead:
• 10-year yield: 4.82%, down ~40bp since 1 October
• $QQQ: -20% from the high
• $SPY: -10% from the high, back where it started the year
• Gold: -3% today, alongside stocks

My read: this is no longer an inflation scare. Bonds are betting the Fed tightens until something breaks, and the market has decided that something is the debt-funded AI build-out.

The economy is not weak. One heavily financed corner of it is being repriced for a higher cost of capital. That is why tech is in a bear market while the Dow barely moved.

What I'm watching:
• 9 Dec dot plot: does the Fed move up to the market?
• High-yield spreads: a break above the 5 Nov high means it is spreading
• Gap fills: ~590 on $QQQ, ~660 on $SPY

In this tape, who funds themselves matters more than who grows fastest. Cash flow over promises.

posts.name: Hedgeye
posts.text:
Benoit Mandelbrot spent a career showing that big gains and losses concentrate into small packages of time.

You can see it setting up in the Risk Range.

When the range on the $VIX starts widening, the volatility of volatility is rising. Moves that used to take weeks start happening in days.

That cuts both ways. A wide range can rip higher. It can also drop a lot further than people expect.

What a widening range does NOT do is give you permission to size up and hope.

What it does tell you
- Expect speed
- Expect bigger daily swings in both directions
- Respect your position MAX more than usual
- Let price come to your levels instead of chasing it

The Machine sells when volatility spikes, often all at once. You don't have to be standing in front of it.

More on how we read ranges at https://app.hedgeye.com/education

$SOXL has virtually collapsed and I know people are hurting. This sucks. No way around that. 

The main $SOXL strategy that I use and have used for many years is called Core Position Trading. 

Core position trading makes money from price swings, not from prices going up. There are no predictions. It’s a mechanical system I use to buy low and sell high.

It is EXTREMELY boring. There are no analysis, no charts, no data points, nothing. It is pure price and volatility. It is not a fast system, you can see from my price targets that sometimes many days, even a week sometimes goes by and nothing happens. It is mechanical to prevent my fear and greed from interfering with my profitability.

Here’s a rough example of how it works.

1. You set a target, a fixed dollar amount to hold in a stock. 

2. Trim above it when the value grows past the target, sell the extra and keep the cash.

3. When the value shrinks, use cash to buy back up to the target.

4. You must have a cash reserve allocation. Cash funds the buys. Without it, you can't use the drops to your advantage.

$SOXL is literally the perfect product for this. It has so many features that make it ideally suited for this system. It has consistently high volatility, high levels of oscillation and mean reversion. 

It is sector based, so it’s not going to disappear, which means by default that it recovers. Not that it recovers to a high, but that it will go up and down and continue to exist.

posts.name: Black Panther Capital
posts.text:
Ok… I haven't been very active over the past few days. Kids have been sick, and work has kept me busy.

But I managed to find some time to put this together.

In my opinion, we're witnessing one of the BIGGEST DISCONNECTS between price and fundamentals I've seen in the market.

Some context first: looking back, I should have taken more profits before this correction started.

This is my personal research and opinion, not financial advice.

So, let's begin:

AI is now a matter of national security. Technology investment has accounted for somewhere between a third and half of US GDP growth this year, depending on how you measure it.

The US cannot afford to fall behind China in this race.

And we're potentially witnessing the biggest industrial transformation in modern history. In my personal opinion everyone knows that and can see that.

Most investors understand the long-term significance. But understanding the opportunity doesn't make the volatility any easier to stomach.

For context my model is built on 2.7 million data points and tracks back the past +70 years.

Right now the market mood is obviously fearful.

Selling pressure is concentrated precisely where the growth is: AI, semiconductors and high-beta technology.

But here's where things get interesting.

The underlying businesses haven't rolled over.

Earnings are still growing. AI spending is still increasing. Even the slowdown analysts anticipate next year implies substantial growth.

The trade is breaking down, but underlying thesis is still very much intact.

And valuations tell an interesting story. $QQQ, technology and beta trades well below earnings. The disconnect here is impressively insane imo.

To be clear, cheaper doesn't necessarily mean cheap. But the valuation picture is very different from what the headline price action might suggest.

The economy isn't breaking either.

My macro model currently reads Goldilocks:

- An economic expansion now 67 months old.
- Growth remains strong and is accelerating.
- None of my five recession indicators are signalling a recession.

Yet the bond market is pricing in something closer to a growth scare: falling yields and widening credit spreads. Another disconnect worth watching.

Under the surface, this looks more like a rotation than a broad market collapse.

The equal-weight S&P 500 is only around 4% below its highs, roughly half the decline in the headline index.

The selling has been disproportionately concentrated in the largest names.

Capital has rotated towards healthcare and consumer staples, and that rotation is becoming stretched.

Even small caps have held up against large caps this month.

There is, however, one significant headwind: interest rates.

Real yields remain close to their highest levels in 20 years. That's a serious obstacle for businesses whose valuations depend heavily on future growth.

So why do I believe a return to risk-on conditions is increasingly plausible in 2027?

A few things stand out in my data:

1. My risk-phase model reconstructs risk-on and risk-off transitions week by week, going back to 1990. 9 of the 12 indexes I track currently have risk-on as the next phase in their historical sequence. For the Nasdaq 100, risk-on followed comparable periods within a year roughly 80% of the time.

2. Inflation swaps are pricing US inflation back towards 2% by late 2027. If that materialises, the interest-rate headwind could begin to ease.

3. Historically, market readings resembling today's have occurred closer to market bottoms than market tops.

4. Semiconductors remain the laggard. They're still in a risk-off phase, and historically, they have tended to take a few months longer to turn.

None of this is a forecast. It's historical precedent, not a guarantee.

So, ehat does this mean for me as a long-term investors?

I don't think the most important question is whether next week is green or red.

It's whether earnings growth and AI infrastructure spending will still be intact in 2027.

posts.name: Gary Black
posts.text:
Many $TSLA and $SPCX investors simply refuse to do the merger math to figure out whether a SPCX-TSLA deal will help TSLA shareholders, who have underperformed the market for 5 years now.  

If you assume an all-stock deal where SPCX acquires TSLA at a 25% nominal premium, and then project out proforma market caps, SPCX needs to issue roughly +52% new SPCX shares to “acquire” TSLA.  That 52% dilution will act as a weight that drags down $TSLA stock price as merger arbs sell forward their $SPCX shares expected to be received on the deal close in maybe 12 months if a deal is announced before year-end.  

That is exactly what has happened in the $MRVL- $LITE deal where $MRVL and $LITE are down -23% and -29% respectively since the deal was announced on Nov 2, as the target $LITE shares are now tied mathematically to $MRVL shares which are being diluted. One can argue TSLA-SPCX won’t be the same since MRVL-LITE is being driven more by the weakness in AI shares generally, but this is the same pattern we see in most dilutive stock-for-stock deals.

Thanksgiving week is historically associated with positive seasonality, but this year's market is telling a very different story.

Monday's monster rally has quickly unraveled, with renewed AI and semiconductor selling threatening another leg lower.

Having traded through the Nasdaq bubble, the financial crisis, and the pandemic, I know that navigating this environment isn't about being perfect. It's about understanding your timeframe, managing risk, and controlling what you can control.

*

Last Friday, with the $VIX above 40, the oscillator at -77, and the market roughly 12% off its highs, I bought $QQQ calls, added some $SPY exposure, and deployed additional capital in my "Blood in the Street" account.

Monday's massive gap-up, accelerated by news of Jensen Huang's reinstatement as $NVDA CEO, provided an opportunity to monetize those positions.

I exited my $QQQ calls with a 250% gain, substantially reduced exposure, and carried very little overnight risk.

Perhaps Monday borrowed too much upside from the rest of Thanksgiving week.

By Wednesday morning, futures were down 130 handles, with numerous semiconductor and AI infrastructure names breaking last week's lows, including $NBIS and $CRWV.

*

Monday's rally stalled precisely around the anticipated $727 resistance near the 8-day MA.

Tuesday's reclaim of $713.50 initially looked constructive, but Wednesday's premarket decline to $705 puts $SPY back in no-man's-land. Can it establish a higher low versus $686?

After rebounding from $606 to $657, $QQQ failed to hold $641, subsequently traded down to $631, and is now around $620 premarket.

Its relative weakness provided clues that Monday's rally was vulnerable. Can it establish a higher low versus $606?

Persistent selling into opening strength remains concerning, with $SMH trading around $407 and approaching the significant $396 low.

What could help the market today? I'm watching two critical sentiment barometers:

*

1. $NVDA: Despite Monday's Jensen-driven euphoria, #NVDA is now within roughly three points of filling its gap.

I hold a small position and will monitor whether the stock can hold or reclaim $115. Establishing a higher low and defending its initial 5- or 15-minute low could provide a constructive signal.

If support fails, I'll exit.

2. $ANT: After opening at $111 versus its $83 IPO price, the stock experienced relentless selling, eventually reaching $75.61 on Tuesday.

While we avoided chasing the initial IPO strength, I think today could present a tactical opportunity.

Holding $75.61 and turning green could help improve broader market sentiment.

*

The bottom line: don't let favorable seasonality, headline-driven optimism, or social media enthusiasm override deteriorating technical conditions.

Look for higher lows, support reclaims, and relative strength before adding exposure. Keep positions manageable and risk clearly defined.

And most importantly, go enjoy Thanksgiving with your family and friends. Food, family, friends, and fun — that's what this week is supposed to be about!

posts.text:
CoreWeave $CRWV is now priced like distressed credit: insuring its debt for five years costs about 13% a year, with its five year CDS at a record 1,314 bps, per Reuters citing S&P Global Market Intelligence.

It's not just CoreWeave. Oracle's five year CDS hit a record 356 bps, and Alphabet and SpaceX also set records overnight, per the same data. SoftBank jumped to 501 bps, its widest since October 2022, per Markit. Reuters says CoreWeave's level implies a 68% chance of default within five years, and its bonds due 2031 now yield almost 18%.

The balance sheet is why credit cares more than equity does. CoreWeave's Q3 10-Q shows about $46.9B of total debt at Sept. 30, up from about $21.4B at the end of 2025, against $4.1B of cash. Property and equipment nearly doubled to $56.8B. That's the neocloud model: borrow against contracts, build fast, collect later.

"Credit markets have continued to price concern about the circular financing and off balance sheet commitments of the hyperscalers," Vantage Point CIO Nick Ferres told Reuters.

Why it matters: the AI buildout runs on borrowed money. Stocks got a relief rally when Jensen returned on Monday; credit never did. A CDS spread is a price, not a default, and CoreWeave has not missed a payment. But if financing gets more expensive, data center timelines and GPU orders are what bend first.

Caveat: CoreWeave isn't paying these prices, and the latest debt raise hasn't brought them to this cost either.

posts.text:
Meta $META and Amazon are reportedly negotiating to end Amazon's blockade of Muse, the AI agent Amazon cut off from its store in September, per a Fortune exclusive.

Per Fortune, the companies have talked multiple times, and the two sticking points are search results and advertising. Amazon's worry is simple: an agent that shops for you can skip the sponsored listings. Fortune says any deal would need sign off from both CEOs, talks are fluid, and it's unclear if or when a deal happens. Both companies declined to comment.

Meta's own numbers show why Amazon can't ignore it. On the Q3 call, Mark Zuckerberg said more than 10 million people in the US and Canada set up Muse in about a month and a half, about 25% use it on any given day, and shopping is the most common use case, with more than a quarter of users shopping and an average purchase over $200. His pitch: "billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together."

Why it matters: this is the biggest test yet of whether the largest online retailer lets an outside agent through the front door, and on what terms. Muse just started checking out at Walmart this week, per The Verge. If Amazon signs on, agentic commerce stops being a demo. Zuckerberg also said on the call that Muse is compute intensive to run, which is why it isn't global yet. More agents shopping means more inference running in data centers.

quoted.text:
I don’t disagree with the premise — although Enron is a bad analogy.  CSCO or Lucent are more appropriate. 

As an example of their circular financing …. Nvidia invests $100M in a customer, and the customer spends $75M of it on Nvidia GPUs
(Assumes a 55% net margin and a 12x forward P/E for NVDA)

Step 1: Nvidia invests

•Cash: −$100M
•New asset: $100M equity stake in the customer, booked as a non-marketable equity investment (or under the equity method if Nvidia owns about 20% or more of customer)

Step 2: The customer buys $75M of GPUs

•Revenue: +$75M
•All-in costs (chips, opex, tax): $33.75M
•Net income at 55%: $41.25M
•Cash collected: +$75M

Step 3: How the market values it

•$41.25M × 12x = $495M of market cap

Scorecard

Amount
Cash out (investment)−$100M
Cash out (all-in costs)−$33.75M
Cash in (chip sale)+$75M
Net real cash−$58.75M
Equity stake on the books$100M
Market cap created$495M
Total paper "value"~$595M

Why it's circular

•Nvidia spends about $59M of real cash and gets about $595M of reported value. That's roughly 10x on the money.
•The $75M of "demand" was Nvidia's own $75M passing through the customer.
•The 12x multiple assumes those earnings repeat. They only repeat if Nvidia keeps writing checks.

Extra kicker: markups

•If the customer's next round comes at 2x the valuation, Nvidia marks the stake up to $200M. That's a $100M non-operating gain on top of the chip profit.
•So the same check pays off twice: once on the chip sale and again on the markup.

posts.text:
🚨 Le bain de sang continue sur le marché US

Fin de bulle ou opportunité d'achat ?

1. Le marché est entrain de pulvériser les actions de la tech 

Les actions mondiales viennent de subir leur pire semaine depuis mars 2020 (-8 %) et les semi-conducteurs leur pire chute depuis 2001 (-18 %), sur fond d'envolée de la volatilité (VIX passé de 19 à 36) et d'écartement des spreads de crédit (ORCL / CWV)

Le rebond de lundi sur la réintégration surprise de Jensen Huang chez $NVDA (+32 %) s'est presque volatilisé, avec Antrhopic qui repasse sous son prix d'IPO, $DELL reperd du terrain malgré un backlog IA massif et l'Asie décroche fortement ce matin (limite risible)

Je vous l'avais dit mais NVIDIA n'est pas tiré d'affaire et je ne croyais pas trop en ce rebond les auditions bipartisanes devant le Congrès la semaine prochaine, durcissement des règles d'exportation visant les data centers étrangers servant la Chine et examen comptable maintiennent une forte prime de risque

2. La Fed devient le juge 

Le marché intègre presque à coup sûr une hausse de taux le 9 décembre et commence à pricer janvier, le chantier IA étant vu comme inflationniste, sur fond de rumeurs de nouveaux droits de douane contre 16 partenaires, here we go again

3. Le vrai basculement du cycle est maintenant le mur de financement, pas la demande

Le marché devient topdown, les capex data centers continuent d'être revus en hausse : plus de 830 Md$ attendus en 2026 (+105 %) puis 1 400 à 1 500 Md$ en 2027 (+85 %). Le sujet n'est plus la demande, mais la facture : ces dépenses absorbent ~100 % du cash-flow opérationnel en 2026 et pourraient monter à 120 % en 2027, contre 25 à 30 % historiquement. Avec ~7 000 Md$ à financer d'ici 2031, la dette atteint ses limites : il faudra davantage de fonds propres et de cash-flow, avec déjà ~370 Md$ de garanties et financements circulaires en jeu

4. C'EST PAS 2000

Le Nasdaq 100 a frôlé le bear market (-20 %) en un mois, au même rythme qu'en avril 2025 ou au printemps 2000, mais autour de 20x les bénéfices attendus contre 60x en 2000

Le marché applique une décote uniforme selon l'exposition aux data centers, sans séparer les néoclouds endettés de l'IA d'entreprise ou de l'inférence. Même le risque politique post-midterms paraît exagéré à court terme, avec un impact net estimé à seulement 2 à 4 % sur le pipeline crédible US

5. Le grand écart entre la bourse et la science 

Le marché doute de la rentabilité du capex alors que le secteur passe d'une consommation libre de tokens à une monétisation centrée sur les résultats mesurables

La consommation quotidienne de tokens a presque décuplé depuis le printemps, les leaders de LLM approchent 150 Md$ de revenus annualisés et les revenus IA nets dépassent 250 Md$ (Difficile d'avoir un chiffre exact)

Google envoi 3 modèles en 3 semaines avec des rumeurs de boucles récursives (Sérieuse chez OpenAI/GOOG/ANT)

Les modèles s'attaquent à des problèmes mathématiques ouverts depuis des décennies (hypothèse de Riemann, VP vs VNP, multiplication de matrices). On parle d'un CHOC total, l'équivalent de 10x la bombe atomique au niveau des maths

6. Les arguments de la street

BULL
A/ Les fondamentaux sont solides, révisions bénéficiaires positives aux US, dans le hardware et les semis, et demande toujours contrainte par l'offre ($DELL plein, primes de 25 à 45 % sur les serveurs IA)

B/ La Visibilité 2027 est verrouillée, les capacités 2027 sont déjà financées et en construction, avec une capacité électrique nord-américaine passant de ~80 à 115 GW

C/  Le marché mondial repasse sous 15x et $NVDA a touché ~8x. Plusieurs segments ont été trop sanctionnés : mémoire/stockage ($SNDK, $STX, $WDC), $DELL, $AVGO, $GEV et le réseau ($CIEN)

BEAR
A/ Fed restrictive en pleine correction, taux longs proches de 5 % et spreads tendus (CDS record sur Oracle, pression sur SoftBank et dette data centers)

B/ Lla croissance du capex va ralentir dès 2028. Une poche d'air sur les commandes d'équipements est possible dé

posts.text: and, for the record, the industry has dropped by a few trillion since i recorded this interview

quoted.text:
Gary Marcus literally explained why AI could be a trillion-dollar mistake. 

> On Steve Eisman's podcast earlier this year, the cognitive scientist who once ran Uber's AI lab put the bill at "one or two trillion dollars," his back-of-the-envelope estimate.

- The idea is scaling. Pour in more data and more GPUs, make the model bigger, and intelligence is supposed to show up.

- He calls it the "trillion pound baby fallacy." A baby weighs 8 lb at birth and 16 lb a month later. Nobody expects a trillion pounds by college.

- His record, in his telling: a 2001 book that predicted hallucinations, a New Yorker piece in 2012, and a 2022 paper called "Deep learning is hitting a wall."

- The industry did not take it politely. He says OpenAI has an emoji for him and Sam Altman called him a troll.

> What LLMs are, to him: "autocomplete on steroids." Great at the fast, statistical "system one" thinking from Kahneman. The slow reasoning part, he says, they have never been good at.

- A lot of smart people with a lot of money made this bet, in his words. Eisman, who bet against subprime before 2008, sat across the table and let him explain it.

Trillions went into making the baby bigger. Marcus is still waiting for it to learn to think.

posts.name: Nick Timiraos
posts.text:
How would the Warsh Fed address market signals saying financial conditions are tightening, with an inflation picture that still looks uncomfortably hot? I wrote about the issue here: https://www.wsj.com/economy/central-banking/wild-market-swings-are-colliding-with-a-fed-bent-on-taming-inflation-73ccab56?st=sd2tND&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink  Despite some easy parallels to the December 2018 situation the Powell Fed faced (A new chair! Trump facing a midterm setback! A hawkish committee! Risk-off!), the inflation backdrop is so different that the comparison struggles to reveal much.

Consider: At that December meeting, the committee's leading intellectual dove, Jim Bullard of the St. Louis Fed, warned colleagues that raising rates risked looking "tone deaf." He presciently predicted that the yield curve would invert if they kept going. But he added a caveat that looks very different today: 

"Taking these types of risks at a meeting like this might be worth it if inflation was running above target and we really felt that we had to be aggressive to keep inflation and inflation expectations contained. But it's not running above target."

TWENTY-FOUR HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 8PM TO 8PM on 11/25/26

The intelligence prong of the case moved in this window. The Journal reported there is no smoking-gun intelligence that Alice Huang was tasked against Jensen Huang, and the intelligence agencies told Congress in a classified briefing that there is no evidence China directed her. The Vice President said on television that Huang was under no investigation and needs no pardon. The Post reported the Pentagon discussed a wartime law as leverage over the board, which the Pentagon denied. Reuters traced a family financing trail for AI servers inside China. The Entity List rule was formally published, the Bessent answer deadline passed with no answer surfacing, and Huang gained a public Senate Banking testimony date on December 3.

THE INTELLIGENCE ASSESSMENT SHIFTS

• The Wall Street Journal reported on November 25, 2026 that Alice Huang was in contact with Chinese intelligence while her affair with Jensen Huang was ongoing, according to people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence, but that there was no smoking-gun intelligence proving she had been actively tasked with collecting information on Jensen Huang or passing along national-security secrets. The Journal article is paywalled; its full text was read in a carriage, and the sourcing is anonymous.
• Per the same reporting, some U.S. officials described her links to Chinese intelligence as circumstantial, given how Chinese business leaders are often compelled to remain in contact with the national-security apparatus, while others said indications she collected and passed information posed a national-security risk regardless of sensitivity.
• The Journal also reported that in March 2026 Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a memo warning President Trump that Jensen Huang was possibly compromised by Alice Huang because of her intelligence connections, though the memo did not definitively say she was a Chinese spy directed to collect intelligence on him.
• Rep. Jim Himes, the incoming House Intelligence Committee chairman, said the intelligence community does not have clear answers on whether she was an active Chinese agent, what information Huang conveyed to her, or what influence she applied. Per the Journal, the administration has shared little of the underlying intelligence with Capitol Hill and a scheduled session the prior Wednesday was postponed.
• U.S. intelligence officials from the FBI, the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence briefed House and Senate Intelligence Committee staff in a classified session on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, one day after President Trump helped secure Jensen Huang's return as CEO, and told them there is no evidence China directed Alice Huang to begin her affair with Jensen Huang or to spy on him. This is the Journal's reporting, carried by concordant relays and a Reuters write-through; the Journal original is paywalled and was not read firsthand. Journal and wire summaries add that the relationship may have been personal, that she had Ministry of State Security contacts, and that no sign of significant intelligence passed was reported.
• The briefing addresses direction and tasking. It does not contradict the dated-contact fact already in the record, which the Journal's companion piece the same day reaffirms.

THE VICE PRESIDENT, IN HIS OWN WORDS

• Citigroup and Standard Chartered are tightening reviews of Southeast Asian datacenter clients, joining regional lenders in demanding disclosure of AI-chip end users and export-control compliance. • Amazon’s first Trainium3 UltraServer submission posted a 2.28x performance-per-dollar advantage over GB300 NVL72 in AgentX’s agentic-inference benchmark. The workload stresses long context, prefix reuse and sub-agent bursts. This is a workload-specific result, not universal GPU displacement, but strengthens the economic case for custom silicon in production inference.

• AI back-end Ethernet switch sales more than doubled in Q3 as scale-up deployments entered volume production. 1.6Tbps port shipments exceeded one million in their first volume quarter. Celestica and Nvidia shared the sales lead; Arista gained two share points and Cisco gained fastest. Networking demand is broadening beyond scale-out fabrics.

• Samsung’s newly disclosed 48GB HBM4E design reaches 17Gbps per pin, versus its previously disclosed 16Gbps maximum—a 6.25% increase. The 2,048-bit interface implies roughly 4.35TB/s of theoretical bandwidth. Its February technical presentation raises the competitive bar for next-generation memory; it does not establish customer qualification or volume-shipment readiness.

• SpaceX outlined more than $50B of investment for its Cochise County supercompute project, including $3.6B for grid upgrades. The design specifies no gas plant, no industrial water use and dry cooling with a closed-loop water system. These remain development commitments, but show how power funding and cooling architecture increasingly shape datacenter execution.

• The FCC conditionally authorized SpaceX’s Starmind constellation of up to one million orbital datacenter satellites. Satellites would primarily communicate through laser links, with radio backup. Approval does not mean imminent compute capacity: launch economics, processor cooling and financing remain hurdles, and debris plans above 600 kilometers still require further approval.

I am fascinated so many people in my replies on this post don’t understand what he’s saying here

This is not shorting a stock

This a shorting a stock you own and avoiding capital gains taxes 

It would be as if I bought Apple 30 years ago, but felt like it was overvalued today, and rather than selling it or hedging with options, I shorted a portion of the stock I owned and avoided long term cap taxes to do it - both short and long at the same time of the same stock

quoted.text: Under IRC 1259(c)(3), shorting against the box triggers no tax on your long shares if you close the short by Jan 30 and hold the longs fully unhedged for the next 60 days. The constructive sale is disregarded, so the low-basis LTCG position stays untouched. Tax arises only on the short’s STCG or STCL when you buy to cover in the open market. Selling the longs realizes the entire LTCG right away. Buying options after that sale requires paying the tax first plus options costs and different rules. The hedge itself is strictly temporary.

Gold has rarely been this oversold:

Gold prices are trading -20% below their 200-day moving average, their largest negative deviation since June 2013.

This marks a sharp reversal from the +45% deviation above the 200-day moving average recorded in January, the largest since the 1970s.

This comes as gold prices have dropped -37% from their January intraday peak, their largest drawdown within a 12-month period since the early 1980s.

By comparison, during the 2008 Financial Crisis, gold prices also declined -20% below their 200-day moving average.

However, the largest such negative deviation was recorded in 1981, at -27%.

Gold is experiencing one of its most severe declines in history.

posts.name: Fireside Alpha
posts.text:
SpaceX’s Riley Trettel says its Arizona data center in Cochise County would lower other residents’ county property taxes by about 20% and lift surrounding small businesses

“These facilities come in and they provide these traditional economic development benefits, like this one in Cochise County bringing in a massive amount of one-time sales-tax revenue, which allows us to completely pay down bonds that the county has already put up and be able to put up new bonds in order to pay for things.

“But also the ongoing property tax of these facilities, being able to pay a greater share of the county’s property taxes so that everyone else’s property taxes can go down. That’s what this facility will do, to the tune of about 20%.

“Those traditional benefits are what are really easy to quantify. But having 6,000 folks working at a facility and needing to eat, needing to get fuel, needing to buy material for the project, that floats all of the small businesses that are in an area.

SpaceX’s Riley Trettel says its Cochise data center could replace members’ electricity bills with checks through $260 million in annual co-op margin

“The benefits of this project at full build-out are pretty massive. On a typical year, folks that are Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative members in Cochise County pay about $130 million a year for power.

The way that we designed this facility is: How can we get that return from our purchase of electricity at very large scale directly back to people in the community where we exist?

“This will be the first project of this kind where we do it at this scale, and we’re extremely excited about it.”

Frank Antenori, whose district includes the site, brought up the county’s tax math during a live Q&A:

“Here’s just something to just chew on. Arizona has an expenditure limit requirement that is placed on counties. If we exceed that expenditure, we have to rebate back to the taxpayers a certain amount.”

“So, if we’re receiving revenue in from SpaceX, by law, we have to offset that to the taxpayers. We have the potential to reduce, based on the projected revenue they’re creating, as much as 20%.”

“Let me just say it again. We could be reducing property taxes across the board in Cochise County, the entire county, by 20% to offset for the revenue here, because we can’t spend all that money. So, we have to give that money back to the taxpayers. The law says we have to.”

Think of it as a yield curve for the cost of compute: the forecasted $/hour price of each chip at every expiry, and whether it's trending up or down. This will change how compute gets bought and financed. Every contract negotiation and every GPU loan will have a market price to check against.

Hundreds of billions of dollars are being committed to compute years in advance. Many of those deals are essentially a levered bet on what GPUs will rent for in the future (what could go wrong lol)

As AI financing sobers up, the labs buying compute, the providers selling it, and the lenders financing it will all need to hedge that risk.

We think compute could become one of the largest financial markets in the world. This launch is Polymarket's first step toward building it.

If you ask yourself the question if recent outages and similar incidents are more frequent than they used to be, or if we just pay more attention, the answer is really clear. Something has changed, just take a look at the November 2026 timeline:

Technical outages

•Nov 12: Microsoft 365 (Outlook, Teams, Copilot) down ~1 day from a latent upgrade defect + capacity issues.

•Nov 13: FAA nationwide ground stop (~4–5 hours) from aging telecom routers/equipment; thousands of flights affected. Workday/payroll also disrupted.

•Nov 15: AWS US-EAST-1 connectivity issues (~2–3 hours) hitting authentication and some services.

•Nov 16: Chase (and related banks) hit by software bug in on-prem hardware (not cyber); United had separate systems outage delaying flights.

•Nov 17: Apple services down from internal update (not cyber). NSA classified network temporarily degraded during scheduled maintenance.

Reported cyber incidents

•Nov 19: JPMorgan, Visa, and Mastercard third-party vendors targeted (n0n group); limited marketing/contact data possibly accessed; core systems and card data unaffected.

•Nov 20: Reported FBI NCIC crime database breach (under investigation) and USDA payment systems intrusion.

•Nov 24: Reported unauthorized access to unclassified CIA/ODNI open-source intel system (no classified data affected). Treasury FinCEN systems also hit, with some taken offline temporarily.

Things will get much worse, before they get better. Are we ready?

The better AI gets at making decisions, the more tempting it’ll be to let it make them for us. Where do we draw the line?

"Handoverism" is the idea that AI could become so capable that we should hand it control of companies, govt, and the biggest decisions we make.

Bill Gurley @bgurley argues that belief in that outcome helps explain why some approaches to AI safety aren’t working. Mustafa Suleyman @mustafasuleyman thinks handing over control is "insane" and says we should be willing to slow down or stop if we can’t prevent the downsides

posts.name: Raoul Pal
posts.text:
Agents started on the 25th November last year. They now exceed all human users on the internet.

That won't surprise a lot of you. Everyone on here has one agent tracking their protein intake, another summarising the newsletters they were never going to read, another replying to emails that someone else's agent wrote, and a head honcho to manage them all.

But step outside this incestuous echo chamber we call X for a second and think about the people you know in real life... (people who work in tech or crypto don't count) Your parents, your neighbours, the friends you grew up with. How many of them use agents? In the US its fewer than one in 10.

It's the iPhone in its first year. Apple sold around 6 million of them, so you probably didnt know anyone who had one, and now almost everyone you know has a smartphone in their pocket. Agents will go the same way... except the iPhone didnt take over half the internet while it was still in a few million hands.

That 57% is coming from a tiny group of early users. As adoption increases, which it inevitably will, the volume will explode beyond anything we can comprehend.

And every one of those agents has to pay for things. Data, compute, the work of other agents, often a cent or less at a time. All of that will happen onchain.

That changes the maths on crypto completely. Every adoption forecast added up the humans who might one day use it. But humans are about to be the minority of users, the same way they're already the minority of the internet... 

Trillions of agents will transact onchain. More times in a minute than you do in a month.

Here are more details on the FCC’s approval for @SpaceX to launch a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind orbital data center satellites.

Under the FCC’s deployment milestones, SpaceX must have the following number of satellites operational by November of each respective year:
• 2033: 1 satellite
• 2035: 100,000 satellites
• 2038: 500,000 satellites
• 2040: 1,000,000 satellites

SpaceX must submit a final orbital debris mitigation plan before deploying satellites above 600 km.

• Satellites will operate at altitudes between 500 and 1,002 km.
• Primary communications will use optical laser links with Starlink satellites.
• Ka-band frequencies are authorized for backup and emergency communications.
• The license term is 15 years.
• No further FCC environmental review is required.

The FCC also denied petitions from Amazon Leo, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society seeking to block SpaceX’s application.

The FCC said the approval will allow SpaceX to pioneer emerging technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence.

Sometimes you win by not losing.

You don’t need to bottom-tick the Qs. You don’t need a strong opinion on NVDA. And you definitely don’t need to press because the last six months whipsawed you flat.

Markets cycle through regimes. Some fit your process. Some don’t. An investor worth his salt needs to know which is which.

We’ve been in an Exuberant-Fragile regime nearly all year — historically our worst regime. Since a clustering of sell signals from our core models in early Oct., we’ve been almost entirely in cash.

Livermore said there’s a time to go long, a time to go short, and a time to go fishing. Few practice the latter today, which is why it's an edge to step away from the screens when there's nothing to do.

Enjoy the holidays. The markets aren’t going anywhere.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
GDP revision highlights a productivity boom!

The Fed Is Fighting a Boom It Doesn’t Understand

This morning’s GDP revision was not a demand scare. It was a supply-side productivity story. Third-quarter growth was raised from 3.4 per cent to 4.3 per cent, led by software and AI equipment investment. Real gross domestic income rose 4.4 per cent. 

Nonfarm business output is now running at 4.9 per cent. Labour productivity, 3.6 per cent on the preliminary reading, should be revised to about 4.8 per cent on 8 December. Unit labour costs, already falling at a 0.7 per cent pace, would decline at about 1.8 per cent. Core PCE inflation in the quarter was unrevised at 2.5 per cent, annualised.

Fact, productivity up, unit labour costs down. This is not inflationary. Wall Street still treats the AI buildout as a three-year product cycle. It is not. It is infrastructure, more like the railroads: a multi-decade build of power, chips and data centres.
Policy is feeding it. 

The key provision of last July’s tax law is 100 per cent expensing, so firms can deduct capital investment immediately. Alongside it came deregulation. A January executive order requires agencies, for each new rule, to identify at least 10 existing ones for repeal. A July order speeds federal permitting for large AI data centres and the energy infrastructure they need.

Alan Greenspan recognised a similar pattern early. At the September 1996 Federal Open Market Committee meeting he argued that official data were understating the gains from information technology, and the Committee held the funds rate at 5.25 per cent even as unemployment fell. In December he asked whether “irrational exuberance” had taken hold. He still held off. A single quarter-point rise in March 1997 was the only tightening for a year and a half. Inflation stayed quiet. The expansion ran on.

This Federal Reserve is doing the opposite. Christopher Waller wants a half-point hike to “shock people.” Alberto Musalem has called for several increases by spring and a real policy rate of 2 to 2.5 per cent.
Potential output is rising, and labour costs per unit are falling. Greenspan trusted that. When will this Fed follow his lead?

THERMAL ALERT: SYZRAN REFINERY, RUSSIA

SITE
• Syzran refinery, Russia, refinery (Rosneft Samara group)
• Owner-operator: Rosneft
• About 8.5 Mt/yr (about 170 kb/d); Syzran, Samara region, on the Volga; the Samara group's second plant, built to supply products to European Russia. Two primary units: CDU-6 at 17,100 t/d (71% of capacity) and CDU-5 at 7,100 t/d (29%)
• Adjacent major refineries within about 10 km: none
• The coordinates below are district-level approximate

DETECTION
• Targeted FIRMS satellite pull, all four sensors, 11/21/26 to 11/25/26: zero hotspots within about 5 km of the plant coordinates, including the night passes covering the raid window; the same VIIRS NOAA-20 pass that caught a Kuibyshev pixel at 11/24/26 7:20 PM EDT covered Syzran minutes apart. Later 11/25/26 passes were still posting at pull time
• The null is evidence against a massive, sustained fire, not against the attack: a brief fire, or one smothered between passes, can evade FIRMS. The NASA GIBS true-color view for 11/25/26 is cloud-covered over the area, so no plume is shown or claimed
• Optical damage assessment is pending: no clear post-event Sentinel-2 scene exists yet

CONFIDENCE
• Event real at the site: HIGH, 85-90%
• Cause (Ukrainian drone strike): HIGH, 90-95%
• Damage (AVT-6 plus sulfur-removal, catalytic reforming, hydrotreating and isomerization units and two tanks, per the General Staff's preliminary list): LOW, 25-40%
• Rationale: eyewitness explosion footage, ASTRA's reporting and Reuters' confirmation of the attack on Syzran's industrial facilities establish the strike and a fire; but the unit list is claimant-only, AVT-6 was already damaged in April and again in September, the mayor calls the damage minor, and the FIRMS null argues against the claimed massive fire

CORROBORATION
• X: footage of a nighttime explosion at the Syzran refinery circulated via ASTRA and the OSINT cluster (NOELreports, Osinttechnical: "ablaze this morning after multiple Ukrainian attack drones hit the facility"); Militarnyi placed the apparent impact area near ELOU-AVT-6, the PGI-DIG/280 installation and the 43-102 catalytic cracking unit. These accounts relay one another and the General Staff; they are one ecosystem, not independent confirmations
• Official: Syzran's mayor Sovetkin acknowledged the attack and called the damage minor (Interfax); Governor Fedorishchev confirmed the regional raid (145+ drones downed, 1 killed, power outages) without naming targets. Rosneft has said nothing
• Web: Reuters confirmed Ukrainian drones attacked industrial facilities in Syzran overnight and that one person was killed in Samara city; it could not independently verify the refinery hits. Bloomberg carries the General Staff's claims for both plants
• Status: VERIFIED (attack and fire at the plant); the claimed unit damage is UNCONFIRMED, and the plant was already effectively offline from the 09/15/26 strike, which damaged CDU-6 while CDU-5 was still under repair from July

WHY IT MATTERS
• With both primary units already damaged in turn this year and the plant effectively offline since September, last night's strike extends the repair clock rather than removing running capacity; the Samara group's combined nameplate is about 310 kb/d, but the barrels at stake are restart timing, not current runs
• The gap between the General Staff's "massive fire" and a clean FIRMS null is the calibration point for this season's damage lists: they have repeatedly run ahead of what satellites and later reporting confirm

posts.name: Hamidreza Azizi
posts.text:
I would be cautious about interpreting #Iran’s recent missile-related statements primarily as an attempt to gain leverage vis-à-vis the United States.

First, one lesson from the recent war should be the limitations of open-source assessments of Iran’s missile capabilities. We all remember how estimates of the proportion of Iran’s missile capabilities destroyed during the war went from 90% to 80% to 70%, only for subsequent developments to call into question the very basis of those assessments.

Second, according to various accounts, Iran has now moved its entire missile production line underground. This makes it considerably more difficult both to assess the pace and scale of missile production and to target the production infrastructure.

Third, we need to take into account the qualitative changes in Iran’s missile program as a result of wartime learning. Recent accounts point to the modification of existing missile systems and the transition of newer systems, such as the Kheibar Shekan 2, from limited to mass production. 

Another important development is Iran’s growing emphasis on protecting its ability to reconstitute its military capabilities. The development of mobile, electro-optical air defense systems and their reported use against American surveillance drones in recent weeks should also be understood in this context.

Of course, none of this means that Iranian claims should be taken at face value. But the growing difficulty of independently assessing Iran’s military capabilities should warrant greater caution in drawing conclusions about their degradation.

There is no contradiction between Tehran’s attempt to gain leverage vis-à-vis Washington and the possibility that its missile capabilities are actually expanding.

别再说马斯克挺黄仁勋只是演戏了。

看看去年黄仁勋亲自飞去 SpaceX 见马斯克的这段视频，这段交情，早就在十年前焊死了。

2016 年，黄仁勋发布全世界第一台 AI 超算 DGX-1。那是当时最顶尖的机器，可发布完，台下一片安静，一张订单都没有。

直到去年 10 月，老黄带着最新一代 DGX Spark 去 SpaceX 找马斯克，当面提起那次冷场，他依然记得清清楚楚：

“全场一片安静。只有一个人例外。那个人，就是你。”

马斯克脱口而出：“我当时觉得，这主意太棒了。”

就凭这一句，那台初代机器被送到了当时的 OpenAI，也顺手点燃了今天的 AI 时代。
再看这个月。

11 月 13 日，黄仁勋还在谷底、能否回归毫无定数，马斯克公开站出来签请愿书；

11 月 23 日，老黄官宣复职，他只淡淡丢下一句：It is done。

转头人就直接现身英伟达总部，和老黄一起庆祝。  

把这两件事放一起看，最戳人的根本不是他们如今多风光，而是这两个时间点——

一次产品还没卖出去，一次人还没回去。两次，马斯克都没等结果。

世人习惯等尘埃落定才选边站，顶级强者之间最稀缺的，恰恰是看不清结局时的那次托底。

posts.name: Handre
posts.text:
In December 2012, Bill Ackman told the world Herbalife was a pyramid scheme. He said that after 18 months of due diligence, he was certain of it, and he had a $1 billion short position to prove it. His case was that distributors earned more from recruiting new distributors than from selling to real customers, and that the company targeted low-income and immigrant communities.

Then Carl Icahn showed up. The two had feuded since a 2003 real estate fight. In January 2013, they sparred live on CNBC, where Icahn called Ackman a "liar" and a "crybaby." Icahn then bought Herbalife stock, reaching 16.5 percent of the company by May 2013, and became its largest shareholder. Every share he bought squeezed Ackman's short. Ackman had started shorting at an average of $47, and by January 2014, the stock had climbed to $83.48.

Ackman kept fighting. A 2016 documentary, "Betting on Zero," followed his campaign. That July, Herbalife agreed to restructure its U.S. business and pay $200 million to compensate consumers. The order forced it to stop rewarding distributors mainly for recruiting a downline, the change Ackman had demanded. The FTC's analysis found that half of Herbalife's "Sales Leaders" earned less than $5 a month on average from product sales.

Ackman was right about the business model, and it did not matter. The stock kept rising, and in February 2018 he quit the trade. Herbalife hit an all-time high that day. Fortune estimated his loss at $500 million or more by 2016, and the stock climbed further after that. Carrying the short cost his fund $20 million a year.

Icahn sold the last of his stake in 2021 with about $1.3 billion in profit. Two years later, a short seller came for him. In May 2023, Hindenburg Research attacked Icahn Enterprises, and over 15 months, his fortune fell by $19 billion.

Herbalife now trades around $12, far below where Ackman shorted it. Ackman had the right thesis and the wrong timing. A short seller faces unlimited losses, monthly carrying costs, and sometimes a rival with deeper pockets who wants to see him lose. 

You can identify a fraud correctly and still go broke waiting for the market to agree.

The lesson from Icahn's side is biblical: "Whatever one sows, that will he also reap."

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Objective Analysis Is Dead on Wall Street

Objective analysis is dead on Wall Street. The job was to question the story. Now Wall Street repeats it, trades it and calls it research. This month it swallowed three stories whole.

First, the spies. A New York Times report that a businesswoman close to Jensen Huang was recruited by China’s spy agency has run through every story on Nvidia. Nvidia says no secrets were compromised, and its board judged Huang no security risk. The accusation still travels farther than the qualification. Durham found the FBI could not corroborate a single substantive allegation in the Steele dossier. The 51 former intelligence officials who flagged the Hunter Biden laptop as Russian disinformation conceded they had no evidence. Credentials did the work evidence could not.

Second, the election. Democrats swept the midterms, and the AI buildout was declared finished. Chip stocks are down 17 per cent since election day. Nobody checked with the customers. Big Tech guides $ 720 billion to $ 740 billion of capital spending this year, and none cut. Rent on a two-year-old H100 hit a record $ 3.46 an hour last week. Nobody pays record rents for a dead technology.

Third, the Fed. Fedspeak is uber-hawkish. Waller wants a half-point hike to “shock people.” Musalem floats four more hikes by spring. Wall Street salutes, with strategists calling for 50 basis points in December.

Monetary policy is a sledgehammer, not a fine-tuning instrument, and it works with long lags. Look through the windshield. There is a glut of oil, and Saudi Arabia has pivoted to fight for market share. West Texas crude is near $ 81, from $ 115 in April. Wholesale gasoline is $ 2.41 a gallon. The crack spread has halved since September. Add the base effects falling off this spring, and any objective view concludes the real fed funds rate is headed to extreme levels: from 0.2 per cent today to roughly 1.9 per cent by mid-2027, with no hike. The Fed is steering by the rear-view mirror.

Three stories, three questions nobody asked. Suspicion passes for knowledge, an election for a valuation, severity for rigour. Objective analysis is dead on Wall Street, and investors are paying for the funeral.

I don’t disagree with the premise — although Enron is a bad analogy.  CSCO or Lucent are more appropriate. 

As an example of their circular financing …. Nvidia invests $100M in a customer, and the customer spends $75M of it on Nvidia GPUs
(Assumes a 55% net margin and a 12x forward P/E for NVDA)

Step 1: Nvidia invests

•Cash: −$100M
•New asset: $100M equity stake in the customer, booked as a non-marketable equity investment (or under the equity method if Nvidia owns about 20% or more of customer)

Step 2: The customer buys $75M of GPUs

•Revenue: +$75M
•All-in costs (chips, opex, tax): $33.75M
•Net income at 55%: $41.25M
•Cash collected: +$75M

Step 3: How the market values it

•$41.25M × 12x = $495M of market cap

Scorecard

Amount
Cash out (investment)−$100M
Cash out (all-in costs)−$33.75M
Cash in (chip sale)+$75M
Net real cash−$58.75M
Equity stake on the books$100M
Market cap created$495M
Total paper "value"~$595M

Why it's circular

•Nvidia spends about $59M of real cash and gets about $595M of reported value. That's roughly 10x on the money.
•The $75M of "demand" was Nvidia's own $75M passing through the customer.
•The 12x multiple assumes those earnings repeat. They only repeat if Nvidia keeps writing checks.

Extra kicker: markups

•If the customer's next round comes at 2x the valuation, Nvidia marks the stake up to $200M. That's a $100M non-operating gain on top of the chip profit.
•So the same check pays off twice: once on the chip sale and again on the markup.

To all newbies :  ⚠️ 3x leveraged ETFs are extremely dangerous if you don’t understand how they work.

They target 3x the daily return, then reset every single day. They do not deliver 3x the long-term return of the underlying index.
Because of the daily reset and compounding, they suffer from volatility decay. 

In choppy or sideways markets, you can lose money even when the index ends flat or up. Losses are amplified fast, and recovery is much harder than with a normal ETF.

These products are built for short-term trading by experienced investors not for beginners or buy-and-hold. Most people who treat them like regular ETFs get hurt.
If you don’t fully understand the daily reset and volatility decay, stay away.

I dont trade these products 👍

The company estimates it would need to stack roughly 75 layers of memory cells to match the density of today’s 10nm-class DRAM. After accounting for other factors, it expects its first product to have 100 layers.

SK hynix said existing equipment can handle 100 layers, but scaling to 200–300 layers and beyond would require the development of dedicated equipment. Longer term, the company plans to explore using multi-deck stacking and hybrid bonding techniques from 3D NAND flash to reach 1,000 layers or more.

posts.text:
Quelle surprise!

France’s government approved the 2026 year-end budget bill, including a deficit of 5.4% of GDP. 

Unsurprisingly, France will not reach its deficit goal of 5%, which is already entirely out of whack, given that the French economy is expected to grow a meager 0.3% this year.

The only reason France’s debt-to-GDP ratio, already close to 120%, is not swelling even faster is inflation, which has averaged 3% since 2022.

Expect big promises from politicians on the unsustainable French budget in the run-up to the presidential elections (starting in April), but don’t forget to look at the hard data.

I don’t know if we will get another European debt crisis next year, but I do know the pressure on the ECB and its monetary policy will keep rising, especially as it signals a tightening bias.

What remains fascinating is that economists, investors and policymakers continue to ‘overlook’ the gigantic French elephant in the room.

And it's not the only elephant present.

BREAKING: US oil prices have recorded 3 drawdowns of at least 20% so far in 2026, matching their 2nd-longest such streak since the 1980s.

2020 was the only year with a longer streak, at 4 such declines, while 1990, 1991, 1998, and 2022 each recorded 3.

Taking intraday prices into account, US oil prices have posted 4 drawdowns of at least 20% this year.

Furthermore, oil prices have seen 8 corrections of 10%+ so far in 2026, their longest such streak since 1986.

The same number of 10%+ drawdowns was posted in 1990, 2004, and 2009.

Year-to-date, oil prices are up +42%, on track for the largest annual gain since 2021.

US oil prices have rarely been this volatile.

posts.name: Diane Swonk
posts.text:
Very different from 1990s boom. Back then, much less concentration of wealth and bigger bang for buck in terms of the surge in employment.  The spend is, after adjusting for actual spending -@BEA undercounting due to competitive pressures & not wanting to reveal plans - BUT employment is small fraction. It was tight labor markets and low inflation that allowed people to develop a cushion. The result is that we did not get a correction in the economy until a year after tech bubble burst. I worry that is could be quicker this time. Offset could be the extent go which is stops crowding out of other investments and keeps firms hiring. That is a hope, not a known. 

The hard part of the 1990s bust was the jobless recovery that followed. Y2K fix and upgrades borrowed from the future. Patching vulnerabilities could do the opposite today. 

Hard to parse but important to understand what happened and why. 

No two business cycles alike. That is the humility of history.

Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly to buy Lukoil’s oil and gas assets outside Russia

Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly’s asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil’s assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC.

The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said.

The deal transfers Lukoil’s international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said.

The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production. (CNBC)

posts.name: Joseph Brusuelas
posts.text:
Want to wish everyone an early Happy Thanksgiving and traditional holiday season.  

Through the end of the year there will be a focus on food and gift prices that are rising. 

Given the successive price shocks over the past five years that makes perfect sense. 

While I understand it's all too easy to look at the $35 Thanksgiving meal with all the trimmings that feeds 10 from Wal-Mart and project wonder about their profitable supply chain, I think it is missing the point. 
 
It’s the little things that we all do around this time. 
 
The handmade sage sausage in the stuffing. The grated orange in the cranberry sauce. The wine infusion in the turkey. The handwritten note for Christmas. 

That is what really matters at the holidays.

The $35 all in via Wal-Mart may appeal to many but I think it angers the majority.

Why?

Because too many households feel pushed into purchasing it due to rising cost of living. 

For those that would put forward solutions to the affordability challenges that sit before the American economy it is something to remember. 

What on the surface appears to be a bargain-that permits many to take part in a way they can't due to economic reasons- it's a not so gentle reminder of our own shortcomings and a type of market failure that all too many will never admit.

So when one looks at sour public attitudes around the economy or rising public inflation expectations it’s the little things in the aggregate that we all too often miss that are the cause of such discontent.

Be creative, innovative and don't be afraid to turn over a table or two of self-important VIP's to restore a semblance  of economic security and price stability. 

As our good friends @nytimes  use  to remind us within the black and white newsprint of an age gone by: 

Remember the neediest at the holidays.

Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans https://cnb.cx/4jBQWiT

posts.name: Joseph Brusuelas
posts.text:
Inflation Rises, Income Stout as US Imposes Section 301 Tariffs

As the economy heads towards the end of 2027, it is running hot amid rising inflation that demands rate hikes from the Federal Reserve.

The question is no longer will the Fed hike at its December meeting. 

It will

The more important question is will it hike at its January and February meeting? If it were not for financial market volatility and the recent decline in oil, gasoline and diesel prices that answer would be an emphatic yes. However, at this point we think that the Fed will hike at its December 2026 and March 2027 meetings with risk of a January hike dependent upon how hot aggregate demand remains and the evolution of the November and December pricing data.

The U.S. October data illustrated two key undeniable facts: aggregate demand is hot and inflation accelerating.  The 0.7% increase in nominal income, the 3.8% rise in the PCE inflation data, household spending and expansionary fiscal policy driven increase of 4.3% GDP in the third quarter of the year all support that undeniable fact.

posts.name: Joseph Brusuelas
posts.text:
Forward Guidance

The PCE data all but locks in a December rate hike. The key question is will the Fed hike again in January and then again in March. We will have to wait to see how the economy and inflation evolve into the New Year and the forward guidance ex-Kevin Warsh the remainder of the Fed heads provide.

The key risks to the inflation outlook remain two of the main drivers-the other being sticky service sector inflation tariffs and energy costs.

Because we simply do not know what, if any, next steps will occur in the Middle East and how the next round of “Section 301” tariffs linked to national security will be implemented despite the recent decline in oil, gasoline and diesel prices, one should anticipate that inflation will remain elevated in 2027.

Our 2027 forecast for the PCE implies an average of 2.9% in the top line and 2.7% in the core and much of that is based on an expected assist from generous base year effects. Based on data ripped from the headlines this morning 20% tariffs on China that could increase to 40% if talks on extending the current trade war truce are not extended, 20% on the E.U. as well as other trade partners like Brazil, India, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam could conceivably result in trade taxes in line with the IEEPA round that the U.S. Supreme Court ruled as unconstitutional in addition to another round of rising energy prices due to the a curtailment supply accompanied by further destruction of production capacity of oil and distillates in the Persian Gulf region that all point to further pass through of such prices increases downstream to American households.

posts.name: Diane Swonk
posts.text:
Inflation hot, spending weak, precautionary savings up

Income rebounded, spending didn't. Real disposable income rose 0.5% in October after a 0.3% drop in September. Dividends were up 1.8% and Social Security 1%. Real consumer spending was flat, and the saving rate jumped to 4.1% from 3.6%. Retailers are leaning on holiday promotions.
Inflation reheated. 

Headline PCE rose 0.3% after 0.5% in September, which is 3.8% from a year ago, the hottest annual pace since May. Core PCE rose 0.3%, or 3.3% from a year ago, the hottest since November 2023. Gains were more dispersed than in September, and the Fed watches that closely.
Food added to the heat. Grocery prices rose 0.4% and restaurants 0.5%. The wholesale food PPI jumped 1.2%, so more food inflation is likely in November and December.

Energy cooled. Lower pump prices could shave 0.2% from PCE in November, but gas tax holidays lapse at year-end.

Two shocks keep prices up. The AI buildout is adding at least 0.8% to the PPI. A new round of Section 301 tariffs starts in the new year, and one tariff hits December 4.
Services stay hot. Super core rose 0.3%, or 3.6% from a year ago. Health care demand is outrunning supply, and the care economy is getting worse.

Real GDP was revised up sharply. Third-quarter growth went from 3.4% to 4.3%, the strongest in three years. Part of the gain was front-running of tariffs and data center inputs. Profits kept soaring, which gives a buffer against an AI correction.

The Fed is in a tough spot. It meets December 8-9 and is expected to raise rates a quarter point. A half-point hike has evaporated, and a dissent in favor of a hold is possible.

Consumers are still spending, but too many are running to stand still. Shocks are now a feature of the forecast, not one-off events.
