posts.name: Kim G C Moody
posts.text:
$158.3 BILLION. That’s how much new fiscal room Ottawa found compared with its spring economic update. And what did it do? It committed 96% of it to new measures.

So much for @MarkJCarney’s vacuous promise to “spend less, invest more.” The Parliamentary Budget Officer’s verdict last week: “This budget spends more, invests more and borrows more.”

It’s Wednesday, which means another edition of my weekly 1-1-1 newsletter: one comment each on taxation, leadership and economics/politics.

This week’s common theme is the unwillingness of leaders to make difficult decisions and properly fix the problems they’ve inherited.

On economics and politics, I examine the PBO’s review of Budget 2026. Without the new measures, this year’s deficit would have been $43.8 billion. Instead, it’s projected at $62.3B. That’s an $18.5B choice in a single year.

Even using the government’s deceptive accounting treatment that splits the budget into operating and capital components, an operating surplus was within reach this year. Ottawa chose to spend its way past it. But, no worries - I’m sure there will be a large reclass soon. 

By 2030-31, the PBO projects annual debt charges of $2,000 per Canadian and per capita liabilities of $74,000, up from $56,000 last year.

Interestingly, recent Angus Reid polling shows that 58% still approve of Carney’s performance, even though more respondents believe his government has hurt rather than helped on spending and the deficit. How much weight are Canadians giving to fiscal management when assessing their government’s performance?

One of my recommendations is a simple windfall rule: when new fiscal room appears, at least half should go toward reducing the deficit.

On leadership, I discuss why the problems you inherit eventually become the problems you own. Every leader inherits organizational baggage, but a workaround isn’t a fix.

Three habits can help:

• Identify the workarounds your team has learned to live with.
• Fix one poor process properly each quarter, with an owner and a deadline.
• Never build a new workaround on top of an old one.

A year into your leadership, nobody remembers who created the problem. They remember who kept it.

On taxation, I revisit the distinction between tax simplification and genuine tax reform, the subject of yesterday’s Financial Post column.

The PBO reinforces my argument: the proposed measures reduce administrative burden but don’t yet address the deeper complexities of our tax system.

Ottawa promises that “deeper reforms will take time and sustained effort.” Yet there’s no expert panel, no mandate and no timeline.

The easy stuff comes with dates and the hard stuff comes with adjectives.

My bonus comment comes from Benjamin Franklin, who wrote in 1737: “Well done is better than well said.”

Nearly 300 years later, it’s still an excellent test of any promise made by a business leader or a prime minister.

Happy reading!

one assumption i want to question about AI is that we'll eventually figure out the “best future” and then the remaining task will be getting everyone to agree to it. people want different things, and what they want can change. where more intelligence will help is in making those differences easier to accommodate.

nick bostrom's influence is worth revisiting on anthropic's ipo day. dario, like many of today’s most influential ai founders and researchers, read his work over a decade ago, and bostrom’s book superintelligence helped define questions the industry still faces. i'd like us to engage just as seriously with the possibilities bostrom explores in deep utopia, his subsequent book which asks what we do after we get superintelligence. some notes from my conversation with @eddylazzarin:

-superintelligence could make radically different versions of the “good life” possible. you might want a 200-year lifespan and a village where nobody carries a phone; someone else might want neural implants. someone else might want to live in vice city (either the real version or just a super realistic matrix-sim). ai could help design the economic arrangements that sustain all of this.

quoted.text:
Ideally the AI trade implodes alot MORE.

The whole AI capex race is fueled by the perception that excessive and durable economic rents will accrue to the first mover to attain a monopoly in *something*.

Is that something AGI?  ASI?  Brand lock-in on the consumer UX?  Who knows.  Does it matter?  One way or another the future being articulated by Silicon Valley is:  You'll cede power (and cash) to platforms controlled by a small group who isnt you, one way or another.

Their race to extract winner-take-most rents is fuelling a huge, potentially redundant, capex boom, with huge opportunity costs.  It has created a nasty externality of crowding out capital access for the rest of the productive economy.  It is reducing the ability of the US to re-industrialise.

Meanwhile, the Western world's fixed capital stock is in a woeful state of underinvestment with 50+ years of "techincal debt" accrued because of structural impediments to building in the real world, and because we outsourced much of the physical economy to the East.

If we want lower structural inflation and higher living standards on a broad basis, we need to invest MUCH MORE in energy, water, basic materials, the industrial supply chain, and real-world  infra like roads, rail, and housing.

So, in a perfect world, AI equities get smoked, the upper leg of the "K" gets a big bad margin call, and the  impulse from AI capex reduces.  Bonus points if we get real anti-trust enforcement as well.

This would free up resources

posts.name: Adam Butler
posts.text:
It breaks your brain, doesn’t it?

It seems Jensen Huang has been negligent on national security at best, and broken many federal laws at worst. But there are no consequences, because stocks can’t be allowed to fall. 
What’s been so fascinating, observing all this from the other side of my own radicalization in 2008, is watching people discover - or perhaps rediscover - that the game is rigged. Many people have unpleasant experiences early in life that create festering anger and cynicism. I didn’t. I led a relatively sheltered life, and thought markets were genuine meritocracies. When Obama bailed out the banks and insurance and mortgage and industrial finance arms of companies in 2008, and the execs all kept their multi-million dollar bonuses, and nobody went to jail, that broke me. I’ve never seen the world in the same way since. And I’ve basically never touched equity markets in my pro accounts again. Because they terrify and disgust me.

To those seeing for the first time how the system really is - I sympathize. I hope you find more healthy and productive ways to cope than I have.

Chinese Refiners Snapping Up Cut-Price Oil to Refill Stockpiles

Chinese state-owned and independent refiners have boosted oil purchases this month, taking advantage of falling crude and transport costs to replenish stockpiles depleted by the Middle East war. 

Unipec — the trading arm of China’s biggest refiner Sinopec — has bought as many as 20 cargoes, usually of about 1 million barrels each, from West Africa for December loading, according to traders. That compares with a monthly average of roughly 20 million to 25 million barrels from the region to all of China.

The Chinese buyers are also snapping up Persian Gulf and Brazilian shipments. Prompt Saudi and Iraqi barrels have been changing hands at $2 to $3 a barrel above the Dubai benchmark on a delivered basis to East Asia, said the traders. (Bloomberg)
